extracted.intended_audience: State environmental agencies, regulated industry stakeholders, environmental advocacy organizations, and legal practitioners participating in EPA CAA section 111 rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards used by EPA in setting standards of performance (BSER) and emission guidelines under Clean Air Act section 111, including how EPA evaluates technologies, costs, representativeness of test data, lead time, and state-plan implementation. Intended to inform how EPA and states determine applicability, stringency, and reasonable compliance pathways for affected sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrapolation from short-term testing to identify BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may extrapolate from testing results, rather than relying on consistent long-term performance, to identify an appropriate system and standard based on that system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by Sierra Club v. Costle (EPA analyzed scrubber performance by considering performance during short-term testing periods). EPA can use short-term test results to infer system performance for standard-setting if representative and justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead time to accommodate development of projected technology
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may authorize lead time in a rule to accommodate the development and adoption of projected or emerging technologies that underpin the chosen system of emission reduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorization for lead time accommodates technology still being developed and allows projected technologies to be considered when determining standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate demonstration may rely on projection for partially-developed systems
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of emission reduction may be deemed 'adequately demonstrated' based in part on projection even if some aspects of the system remain in development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may determine adequate demonstration based on some amount of projection and consider projected technology performance when setting standards and lead times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost reasonableness constraint (no exorbitant or survival-threatening costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: In establishing standards, EPA must consider costs, and costs may not be 'exorbitant' or 'greater than the industry could bear and survive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited cases include Lignite Energy Council and Portland Cement Ass'n v. EPA. Legislative history acknowledges cost consideration but treats costs as a normal expense of doing business; EPA must balance statutory factors and avoid imposing costs that would be unreasonably burdensome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrator discretion in weighting statutory factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Congress did not assign specific weights to the statutory elements (cost, energy, non-air quality health/environmental impacts), the Administrator has discretion to emphasize or deemphasize particular factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's balancing is constrained by requirements of reasoned decisionmaking but not by any prescribed weights (see New York v. Reilly; NRDC v. EPA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of technological innovation within statutory balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Technological innovation is an allowable subfactor within the statutory balancing of cost, energy, and non-air quality health and environmental factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sierra Club v. Costle recognizes that promoting innovation can be part of the 'best' balancing and standards may be designed to encourage development of new control techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider non-GHG air pollutants and non-air quality impacts when evaluating controls
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating a system of emission reduction (BSER), EPA may consider the effects of controls on non-GHG air pollutants and on non-air quality health and environmental impacts alongside effects on greenhouse gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA has discussed such effects together in prior rulemakings (e.g., oil and natural gas sector climate review) and may analyze co-benefits and tradeoffs across pollutant and health/environmental categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representativeness criteria for sampled/tested sources
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing the representativeness of a tested source, EPA may consider variables such as feedstock, operation, size, and age; a sample of one can be generalized when it is shown to be representative along relevant parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nat'l Lime Ass'n v. EPA supports generalizing from a single representative sample; EPA should justify representativeness by comparing relevant parameters of the tested unit to the regulated industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'designated facility' (40 CFR 60.21a(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'designated facility' means any existing facility that emits a designated pollutant and would be subject to a standard of performance for that pollutant if the existing facility were an affected facility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory definition used to determine which existing plants are covered for purposes of applying emission guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: New vs. existing source determination based on EPA proposal date
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 111, whether a source is 'new' or 'existing' (and thus potentially a designated facility) is determined by the date that EPA proposes to establish standards of performance for new sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This timing rule affects classification and whether a facility is subject to new-source standards or treated as an existing source for guideline purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: EPA's primary regulatory role under section 111(d) for existing sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Although States set the specific rules governing existing plants, EPA retains the primary regulatory role in section 111(d) by determining the amount of pollution reduction that must ultimately be achieved and the BSER adequately demonstrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: West Virginia v. EPA explains the allocation: EPA identifies BSER and permissible level; States submit plans to adopt and enforce emissions restrictions so as not to exceed that level (see 40 CFR 60.22(b)(5), §§60.23, 60.24).

rubrics_metrics.name: State plan submission requirement to meet EPA-established permissible levels
rubrics_metrics.description: States submit plans containing the emissions restrictions they intend to adopt and enforce to ensure they do not exceed the permissible level of pollution established by EPA under section 111(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States' plans are evaluated against EPA's determination of the permissible level and the BSER; statutory citation: 42 U.S.C. 7411(d)(1) and implementing regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less stringent standards for particular units when costs differ (40 CFR 60.24a(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: States may apply a less stringent standard of performance to particular affected EGUs if the state can demonstrate a fundamental difference between the costs EPA considered and the costs to that particular unit that make the more stringent degree unreasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if costs make it unreasonable for a unit to meet emission limitation corresponding to 40% natural-gas co-firing, a state may set a lower co-firing level after demonstrating cost differences; states should consider whether co-firing at lower levels is reasonable for units that cannot cost-reasonably achieve the higher level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability exemption for sources retiring before a specified date (HRI example)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA may exempt certain technologies or measures (e.g., heat rate improvement (HRI)) from applicability for sources that will retire before a specified date because such measures may yield few emission reductions and could have adverse effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA found HRI inappropriate for sources retiring before January 1, 2032 due to limited CO2 reductions and potential rebound effects; this exemption does not conflict with states' ability to consider remaining useful life for particular sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of the 'rebound effect' when evaluating efficiency measures
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must consider that some efficiency measures (like HRI) can trigger a rebound effect, where CO2 emissions increase rather than decrease as a consequence of imposing the technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebound effect analysis should inform whether a measure is appropriate for inclusion in BSER or emission guidelines, particularly for units with different operating horizons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remaining useful life of particular sources (RULOF) is a state-level consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The RULOF provision is intended to address specific conditions of particular sources when a state applies a standard of performance, whereas EPA determines general regulation of the source category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RULOF applies only in state implementation of standards to account for peculiarities of an individual unit's remaining life; EPA-level exemptions (e.g., for retiring-sources) are separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical amortization period assumptions for capital costs (general and CCS)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA typically assumes capital costs can be amortized over 15 years; for carbon capture and storage (CCS), EPA generally assumed a 12-year amortization period because the IRC section 45Q tax credit is available for the first 12 years of operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amortization assumptions affect cost-per-ton calculations and cost reasonableness analyses for technologies such as CCS; EPA explains deviations where tax incentives alter the effective amortization horizon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on relying solely on EPAct05-assisted project experience
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's prior legal interpretation is that EPAct05 provisions preclude relying solely on the experience of facilities that received EPAct05 assistance to determine whether technology is adequately demonstrated, but EPA may rely on such facilities in conjunction with other information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing adequacy of demonstration for CCS or other technologies, EPA should combine EPAct05-assisted project data with other broader evidence rather than treating assistance-funded projects as dispositive by themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operating availability metric for capture equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Operating availability is defined as the percent of time that the CO2 capture equipment is available relative to its planned operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metric is used to characterize realistic capture equipment performance and availability assumed in modeling and feasibility assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of turndown and duty cycle for operational characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Turndown: the ability of a facility to reduce process values (e.g., flowrate) relative to maximum instantaneous capability, typically expressed as a ratio and limited by a lower threshold. Duty cycle: the ratio of gross electricity generated relative to potential generation at nameplate capacity, indicating cycling/load-following behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These operational definitions are used to evaluate feasibility and expected performance of controls and capture systems under real-world operating patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER may be projected forward (look to reasonably projected future state of the art)
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting the best system of emission reduction, EPA may look toward what may fairly be projected for the regulated future, rather than only the current state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portland Cement Ass'n v. Ruckelshaus supports projecting forward to reasonably anticipated future technology when identifying BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of sequestration transport and storage feasibility and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considers site-specific characterization of saline formations for sequestration suitability and storage capacity, and models pipeline/transport timelines and permitting durations when assessing CCS feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representative timelines referenced include an 18-month construction period for pipelines and 1.5 years for permitting in EPA's representative timeline; project-specific permitting and construction may vary and can begin earlier depending on ongoing projects.
